title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 58–59 (editorially reviewed)
description: Units 58–59 reviewed against the textbook teaching pages, diagrams, illustrated exercises, published answers and British English phonemic index. Unit 58 covers common prefixes and meaning changes; Unit 59 covers suffixes, related word classes and natural collocations. All learning content is in English, with Brazilian Portuguese restricted to pt. Original example sentences are used.
sourceNotice: The supplied textbook was used for source-target coverage and phonemic-index checks; its exercises and illustrations are not reproduced. Vocabulary from exercises is distinguished in notes. Two sourced collocations were added from the published answer key; careful is a clearly identified pedagogical extension.

audit.scope: Compared Unit 58 teaching page and visual on printed p. 122 (PDF p. 123), exercises 58.1–58.4 on p. 123 (PDF p. 124); Unit 59 teaching page and images on printed p. 124 (PDF p. 125), exercises 59.1–59.4 on p. 125 (PDF p. 126), the published answer key on printed pp. 156–157 (PDF pp. 157–158), and available British English IPA in the phonemic index (PDF pp. 160–170). Checked translations, examples, morphological rules, word stress, item IDs and English-only content.
audit.pronunciation: British English IPA, with phonemic-index checks for indexed headwords (PDF pp. 160–170). Stress in multiword expressions is an editorial reading guide and may vary in connected speech.
audit.cannotGuarantee: Local JSON parsing, types, ID uniqueness, original ID preservation and English-only checks have been performed. Import into VocabLab 1.2 Lite, browser speech synthesis, recording, adaptive-review behaviour and backup/restore were not tested. Human editorial approval is pending.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Source teaching pages and pictures, full exercises and published answers, book phonemic index where available, entry-by-entry language and usage review, local JSON/ID/type checks.
editorialReview.notes: Original 98 item IDs, two unit IDs and package ID preserved. Two additional exercise-derived collocations: u59-sunny-smile and u59-fast-worker. The item u59-careful is an explicitly labelled pedagogical extension. IPA outside the book index has not been independently verified by a pronunciation dictionary.

units.title: Unit 58 — Prefixes
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 58, printed pp. 122–123 (PDF pp. 123–124); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: Nina met her ex-wife at a family celebration.
items.note: The prefix ex- marks a former relationship or role. An ex-wife was previously married to the person being discussed; the hyphen is part of this spelling.

items.example: Her ex-boyfriend now lives in another town.
items.note: Ex-boyfriend means someone who was a boyfriend in the past but is not now. The source table introduces ex- before nouns.

items.pt: pela metade do preço; com 50% de desconto
items.example: The blue bags are half-price this week.
items.note: Half-price means costing 50% of the normal price. The compound is hyphenated in the source and can follow be: The tickets are half-price.

items.pt: meia hora; com duração de meia hora
items.example: We took a half-hour break after lunch.
items.note: Half-hour means a period of 30 minutes. Use a half-hour break or a half-hour journey before a noun; a half hour can stand alone without the hyphen.

items.example: The meeting is informal, so you can wear jeans.
items.note: The negative prefix in- turns formal into informal. The book contrasts informal jeans and trainers with more formal clothes.

items.example: It is impossible to read this tiny writing from here.
items.note: The prefix im- means not here: possible becomes impossible. The book explains this through things a person cannot do.

items.pt: onde não se permite fumar; para não fumantes
items.example: We booked a non-smoking room at the hotel.
items.note: Non- expresses not or an absence of a property. Non-smoking describes an area, room or restaurant where smoking is not allowed.

items.pt: pré-escolar; referente à idade anterior à escola
items.example: The library has activities for pre-school children.
items.note: Pre- means before. Pre-school describes children below school age; the source spells this compound with a hyphen.

items.example: Please pre-heat the oven before making the biscuits.
items.note: Pre- means beforehand: pre-heat an oven before cooking. The source uses pre-heat; modern dictionaries also list preheat without a hyphen.

items.example: I made several mistakes, so I need to redo the exercise.
items.note: Re- means again. Do becomes redo; irregular past and past participle: redid and redone. The source contrasts redo and rewrite.

items.example: Could you rewrite this message more clearly?
items.note: Re- indicates repetition: rewrite means write something again. Irregular forms: rewrote, rewritten; the source index stresses the first syllable.

items.example: The children were unhappy about the change of plans.
items.note: Un- means not here: unhappy is the opposite of happy and is close in meaning to sad.

items.example: That old bridge is unsafe in strong winds.
items.note: Un- makes the opposite of safe. Unsafe means dangerous, as in the warning sign illustrated in the teaching section.

items.example: You need formal clothes for the ceremony.
items.note: Formal clothes include suits or other clothing appropriate for particular occasions. Contrast formal and informal.

items.example: He wears formal clothes when he meets customers.
items.note: This noun phrase is presented on the teaching page. Formal modifies clothes, which is always plural in this sense.

items.example: I usually wear informal clothes at home.
items.note: Informal clothes are casual clothes, such as jeans and trainers in the textbook explanation. Trainers is British English for sports shoes.

items.example: Is it possible to arrive before midday?
items.note: Possible describes something that can be done or may happen; impossible adds the negative prefix im-.

items.example: We had lunch in a non-smoking restaurant.
items.note: A non-smoking restaurant does not allow smoking. The adjective non-smoking describes the restaurant's rules, not an action performed by the building.

items.example: The museum has a special area for pre-school children.
items.note: Pre-school children are too young to attend school. The teaching page uses pre-school with children.

items.pt: pela metade do preço na liquidação
items.example: These shoes are half-price in the sale.
items.note: Exercise 58.1 uses the source phrase half-price in the sale. A sale is a period when shops offer reduced prices.

items.example: He was unhappy at school until he made some friends.
items.note: Exercise 58.1 reinforces unhappy as a feeling in a school setting. Compare happy at school.

items.example: Her ex-husband takes the children to school on Fridays.
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces ex-husband for meaning inference: a man who was once married to someone but is no longer their husband.

items.example: I always get pre-exam nerves the night before an important test.
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces pre-exam nerves. Pre- means before, and nerves here means feelings of nervousness.

items.example: Your address is incorrect on this form.
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces incorrect: not correct. The prefix in- is used here, not un-.

items.example: There are still five unread emails in my inbox.
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces unread as an adjective meaning not yet read. Here read is pronounced /red/, unlike present-tense read /riːd/.

items.example: Please retell the story in your own words.
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces retell: tell a story again. The irregular past and past participle are retold.

items.example: I have a half-brother on my father’s side.
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces half-brother: a brother with one parent in common. Contrast stepbrother, related by a parent's marriage rather than shared parentage.

items.example: She left an unfinished letter on the desk.
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces unfinished: not completed. It can modify a letter, task or other piece of work.

items.example: Do you have a non-alcoholic drink?
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces non-alcoholic to describe a drink without alcohol. The prefix non- expresses the absence of alcohol.

items.example: I often reread useful notes before a test.
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces reread, meaning read again. Present /ˌriːˈriːd/ and past /ˌriːˈred/ have the same spelling but different final vowel sounds.

items.example: Can you resend the email with the correct attachment?
items.note: Exercise 58.3 introduces resend: send again. Its irregular past and past participle are resent; context distinguishes them from resent meaning feel bitterness.

items.example: These shoes are uncomfortable for long walks.
items.note: Exercise 58.4 asks for the negative of comfortable: uncomfortable. English uses un-, not in-, with this base adjective.

items.example: It is impolite to interrupt another person.
items.note: Exercise 58.4 asks for the negative of polite: impolite. Here im- forms the opposite and means not polite.

items.example: There was an unpleasant smell in the kitchen.
items.note: Exercise 58.4 asks for the negative of pleasant: unpleasant. English normally uses un- rather than in- with pleasant.

items.example: The grey walls make the room unattractive.
items.note: Exercise 58.4 asks for the negative of attractive: unattractive. This uses un-, not in-.

items.example: This chair is comfortable for reading.
items.note: Comfortable is a base adjective for exercise 58.4. It contrasts with uncomfortable, which is made with un-.

items.example: The receptionist was polite to everyone.
items.note: Polite means showing good manners. It is the base of impolite in exercise 58.4; be polite to someone is a common pattern.

items.example: We had a pleasant walk in the countryside.
items.note: Pleasant describes something enjoyable or agreeable. It becomes unpleasant with un- in exercise 58.4.

items.example: The old town is attractive to visitors.
items.note: Attractive describes something appealing. Adding un- produces unattractive, as practised in exercise 58.4.

items.example: Your first answer was correct.
items.note: Correct is the base adjective in the exercise 58.3 example incorrect answer. The negative is incorrect.

items.example: My ex-boss sent me a message yesterday.
items.note: The Over to you section suggests ex-boss as another example of ex-: someone who was your boss in the past.

items.example: We bought some water at half-time.
items.note: The Over to you section includes half-time in a football match. This means the break between the two halves of a game.

learningObjectives: Understand that prefixes appear at the beginning of a word and can change its meaning.
Recognise ex- before nouns for a former relationship or role, as in ex-wife, ex-boyfriend and ex-husband.
Use half- to express 50% in half-price, half-hour, half-brother and half-time, without confusing different meanings.
Distinguish negative prefixes in-, im-, non- and un- using the specific word forms supported by the source.
Use pre- for before and re- for again, including pre-school, pre-heat, redo, rewrite, retell, reread and resend.
Work out the meanings of prefixed words practised in exercises 58.1–58.4, including unread, unfinished and non-alcoholic.
Recognise when compounds take a hyphen and use a dictionary when the spelling is uncertain.

units.title: Unit 59 — Suffixes
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 59, printed pp. 124–125 (PDF pp. 125–126); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: My grandfather was a worker in a local factory.
items.note: The suffix -er forms a noun for a person who works. The source teaches worker and the phrase hard worker.

items.example: My aunt is a hard worker and rarely rests.
items.note: A hard worker is someone who works a lot or makes a strong effort. Hard describes effort, not difficulty.

items.example: My cousin is a swimmer and trains each morning.
items.note: Swim becomes swimmer: double the final m before -er. This noun names a person who swims.

items.example: Our instructor taught us how to ski.
items.note: Instruct becomes instructor. The ending -or names a person who teaches or gives practical guidance.

items.example: Our cooker stopped working last night.
items.note: A cooker is a kitchen appliance used to cook food, particularly in British English. A person who prepares food is a cook, not a cooker.

items.example: You can use a calculator for this test.
items.note: Calculate becomes calculator. The ending -or can refer to a machine or other object as well as to a person.

items.example: There is a gas cooker in the new kitchen.
items.note: A gas cooker is a cooker powered by gas. The teaching page shows an example of this appliance.

items.example: The golf instructor helped me with my first lesson.
items.note: Exercise 59.1 illustrates a golf instructor. The instructor teaches or helps someone play golf.

items.example: This website is useful for students.
items.note: Use becomes useful. The suffix -ful makes an adjective indicating usefulness or value in a particular context.

items.example: There are beautiful flowers in the park.
items.note: Beauty becomes beautiful, with a spelling change from y to i. Beautiful is an adjective describing someone or something pleasing to see.

items.example: The torch is useless without batteries.
items.note: Use becomes useless with -less, meaning without useful effect. Compare useful and useless.

items.example: The journey seemed endless to the children.
items.note: Endless means seeming to have no end. It is often an exaggeration for something that takes a very long time.

items.example: She gave me useful information about the course.
items.note: Useful modifies the uncountable noun information. Do not use informations when talking generally about facts or advice.

items.example: This is a beautiful photo of your family.
items.note: The teaching page uses beautiful photo. Beautiful describes the photo; the plural is beautiful photos.

items.example: The old guide is a useless book for modern travellers.
items.note: A useless book gives no relevant help or value for a particular purpose; it is not necessarily bad in every context.

items.example: Please walk quickly or we will miss the bus.
items.note: Quick becomes quickly with -ly. Quickly is an adverb and can describe how someone moves or acts.

items.example: The children played happily in the garden.
items.note: Happy becomes happily: replace final y with i before adding -ly. Happily means in a happy way, not necessarily fortunately.

items.pt: feliz no casamento; vivendo um casamento feliz
items.example: My grandparents are still happily married.
items.note: Happily married means married and happy together. The adverb happily modifies married, and the source uses this combination.

items.example: Music brings her a lot of happiness.
items.note: Happy becomes happiness: final y changes to i before -ness. Happiness is an abstract, usually uncountable noun.

items.example: He spoke about his sadness after leaving home.
items.note: Sad becomes sadness. The suffix -ness makes an abstract noun from an adjective.

items.example: She smiled with happiness when she heard the news.
items.note: The textbook uses smiling with happiness. Happiness is a noun, so with happiness is a prepositional phrase.

items.example: They said goodbye with great sadness.
items.note: The teaching page uses with great sadness when describing a sad farewell. Great intensifies the noun sadness.

items.example: The island has several sandy beaches.
items.note: Sand becomes sandy with -y. It is an adjective for a place with a lot of sand.

items.example: We ate outside on a sunny morning.
items.note: Sun becomes sunny, with a doubled n. Sunny describes a day with sunshine; exercise 59.2 also allows sunny smile in a figurative sense.

items.example: We found a quiet sandy beach.
items.note: The source shows a sandy beach. Sandy describes the beach as having sand rather than only rocks or stones.

items.example: A sunny day is perfect for a picnic.
items.note: Sunny day appears in the source and is pictured in exercise 59.1. Sunny means with sunshine.

items.example: I need a bottle opener for this bottle.
items.note: Exercise 59.3 forms opener from open. A bottle opener is a device for opening bottles, especially bottles with caps.

items.example: I slept badly because of the noise.
items.note: Exercise 59.3 forms badly from bad. In I slept badly, the adverb describes how the person slept.

items.example: The assistant was very helpful when I had a problem.
items.note: Exercise 59.3 forms helpful from help. A helpful waiter gives useful information or assistance to customers.

items.example: Thank you for your kindness yesterday.
items.note: Exercise 59.3 forms kindness from kind. The suffix -ness makes a noun meaning the quality of being kind.

items.example: He lost his keys because he was careless.
items.note: Exercise 59.3 forms careless from care with -less. It means not giving enough attention or care.

items.example: Read your answers again to avoid careless mistakes.
items.note: Careless mistakes are errors caused by a lack of attention. This expression is reinforced in exercise 59.3.

items.example: It is windy by the coast this afternoon.
items.note: Exercise 59.3 forms windy from wind. Windy describes weather with a lot of wind.

items.example: We found the address easily with a map.
items.note: Exercise 59.3 forms easily from easy: replace the final y with i before -ly. It means without much difficulty.

items.example: We need a builder to repair the wall.
items.note: Exercise 59.3 forms builder from build with -er. A builder is a person who constructs or repairs buildings.

items.example: The hotel room has a hair dryer.
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces hair dryer as something used to dry hair. The ending -er names a device here.

items.example: A traveller asked me for directions.
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces traveller as a person who travels. Traveller with double l is the usual British spelling.

items.example: Please speak slowly during the lesson.
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces slowly, the adverb from slow. Compare quickly from quick on the teaching page.

items.example: She is hopeful about her new job.
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces hopeful, meaning full of hope or feeling that something good may happen.

items.example: We stayed home on a rainy Saturday.
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces rainy, an adjective meaning with a lot of rain or characterised by rain.

items.example: The short test was completely painless.
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces painless, meaning not causing pain. The ending -less indicates an absence of pain.

items.example: Can you find the tin opener in the drawer?
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces tin opener, British English for a device used to open food tins. Can opener is also common.

items.example: Her sister wants to become a footballer.
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces footballer, a person who plays football. The suffix -er names the player.

items.example: We drove through snowy hills on our holiday.
items.note: Exercise 59.4 introduces snowy for weather or places where snow is present or falling.

items.example: Our electric cooker is easy to clean.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 combines electric and cooker. A cooker is an appliance, unlike cook, which can mean the person.

items.example: He plays the electric guitar in a band.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 combines electric and guitar. Electric describes the instrument; it is not a new suffix form.

items.example: Leo is a fast swimmer but a slow runner.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 allows fast swimmer. Fast describes the swimmer's speed; compare good swimmer on the teaching page.

items.example: This is a useful book for beginners.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 allows useful book. A useful book helps someone complete a task or learn something.

items.example: They had endless fun playing outside.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 matches endless with fun. Fun is usually uncountable in this sense.

items.example: We are expecting sunny weather tomorrow.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 includes sunny weather. Weather is normally uncountable: sunny weather, not a sunny weather.

items.example: There is a beautiful picture on the wall.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 permits beautiful picture. Picture is countable and can mean a drawing, painting or photograph.

items.pt: ideia inútil; ideia que não funciona
items.example: That was a useless idea because it did not solve the problem.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 includes useless idea, meaning an idea that is no help in solving a problem.

items.example: The little girl has a beautiful smile.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 allows beautiful smile. Here beautiful describes the person's smile, not their appearance generally.

items.example: A fast car passed the bus on the road.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 allows fast car. Fast can be an adjective or an adverb, but fastly is not standard English.

items.example: This opener is broken, so we need another one.
items.note: Opener is the device noun appearing within bottle opener in exercise 59.3 and tin opener in exercise 59.4.

items.example: Be careful when you carry the hot pan.
items.note: Careful contrasts with careless and illustrates the opposite meaning of -ful and -less. It is a supporting pedagogical extension; only careless is explicitly requested in exercise 59.3.

items.example: Her sunny smile made everyone feel welcome.
items.note: Exercise 59.2 explicitly allows sunny smile. Sunny is figurative here: cheerful and friendly rather than literally full of sunshine.

items.pt: pessoa que trabalha rapidamente; trabalhador(a) rápido(a)
items.example: Maya is a fast worker and finishes her tasks early.
items.note: The answer key for exercise 59.2 allows fast worker. Fast relates to speed; hard worker emphasises effort and diligence.

learningObjectives: Identify suffixes at the end of words and recognise how they change meaning or word class.
Distinguish -er/-or for people (worker, swimmer, instructor, builder) from -er/-or for devices (cooker, calculator, opener).
Understand -ful and -less in adjectives such as useful, beautiful, useless, endless and helpful.
Use -ly to create adverbs, including quickly, happily and easily, and apply relevant spelling changes.
Create abstract nouns using -ness, as in happiness, sadness and kindness.
Recognise -y adjectives for weather or physical features, such as sandy, sunny, windy, rainy and snowy.
Understand exercise-derived word forms such as bottle opener, careless, builder, traveller, hopeful and painless.
Use natural noun phrases including hard worker, fast worker, gas cooker, electric guitar, useful book and sunny smile.
Distinguish cooker (an appliance) from cook (a person), and contrast hard worker (effort) with fast worker (speed).
